titulo: Who I am: Sein: to be

aula.objetivo: Introduce yourself, ask for a name and where someone is from, and use «sein» in the present, with «du», «ihr» and «Sie».

blocos.contexto: At a language school in Berlin, the teacher welcomes a new student. She addresses him as «Sie». Later he talks to a classmate, using «du».

linhas.ru: — Guten Morgen! Sind Sie Herr Silva?
linhas.en: — Good morning! Are you Mr. Silva?
linhas.audio: Guten Morgen! Sind Sie Herr Silva?

linhas.ru: — Ja, ich bin Paul Silva. Ich bin aus Brasilien.
linhas.en: — Yes, I am Paul Silva. I am from Brazil.
linhas.audio: Ja, ich bin Paul Silva. Ich bin aus Brasilien.

linhas.ru: — Freut mich, Herr Silva! Ich bin Frau Becker.
linhas.en: — Nice to meet you, Mr. Silva! I am Mrs. Becker.
linhas.audio: Freut mich, Herr Silva! Ich bin Frau Becker.

linhas.en: — Nice to meet you too, Mrs. Becker!

linhas.ru: — Hallo! Ich bin Lea. Bist du auch hier?
linhas.en: — Hi! I am Lea. Are you here too?
linhas.audio: Hallo! Ich bin Lea. Bist du auch hier?

linhas.ru: — Ja, ich bin hier. Ich bin ein bisschen müde.
linhas.en: — Yes, I am here. I am a little tired.
linhas.audio: Ja, ich bin hier. Ich bin ein bisschen müde.

linhas.ru: — Wir sind hier. Wir sind glücklich!
linhas.en: — We are here. We are happy!
linhas.audio: Wir sind hier. Wir sind glücklich!

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: «sein» is the German verb for «to be», and it reads «zine». STEP 2: «sein» is irregular and changes a lot, like English «am / are / is». Listen to the forms: «ich bin», «du bist», «er, sie, es ist», «wir sind», «ihr seid», «sie sind». Watch out: «sind» reads «zint» and «seid» reads «zite». STEP 3: use «sein» to say who you are: «Ich bin Brasilianer» or «Das ist Lea». STEP 4: use it also to say how you are or where you are: «Ich bin müde» and «Wir sind hier». Just like English «to be», one verb does all of these jobs. STEP 5: to make a negative, put «nicht» after the verb: «Ich bin nicht müde». STEP 6: in a yes/no question, the verb goes to the front: «Bist du müde?». Answer: «Ja, ich bin müde.» or «Nein, ich bin nicht müde.»
blocos.comparacao: English has one verb for this, «to be», and German has one too: «sein». The catch is that each person has its own very different form, and you have to memorise them, just as you do with «am / are / is» in English, only with more forms.

erros.motivo: Each person has its own form. With «ich», the form is always «bin».
With «wir», the form is «sind». The form «ist» belongs to «er», «sie» and «es».
The verb stays in the second position, and the «nicht» comes after it.

blocos.titulo: You, you all, you (formal): du, ihr e Sie
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: to talk to ONE person you are close to, such as a friend, family member, child or young colleague, use «du». STEP 2: to talk to SEVERAL people you are close to, use «ihr» (like «you all» or «you guys»). STEP 3: to talk to someone you do not know well, or to show respect, use «Sie», which reads «zee». It works for sir, madam or ladies and gentlemen, one person or several. In writing, formal «Sie» always starts with a capital S. STEP 4: with «Sie» the verb has the same form as for «they»: «Sie sind» and «Wie heißen Sie?». STEP 5: when in doubt, use «Sie». The other person will offer you the «du» when they want to.
blocos.comparacao: English has just one «you» for everyone. In German, the choice between «du» and «Sie» is compulsory, and it changes the verb in the whole sentence.

erros.motivo: With «Sie» the verb stays in the plural, even for one single person.
With «du», the form of «sein» is «bist». «Sind» belongs to «wir» and «sie».

itens.explicacao: You hear «du bist»: the form «bist» goes with «du». «Ich bin» and «wir sind» have other sounds.
The beginning is «veer zint»: with «wir», the form is «sind». In «Ihr seid» you would hear «zite».
Write «bin» with «i» and «müde» with «ü». The «ü» is «oo» with the tongue in the «ee» position, which you practised in lesson 1.
With «ich», the form of «sein» is «bin». The form «bist» belongs to «du» and «ist» belongs to «er».
With «du», the form of «sein» is «bist». The form «bin» belongs only to «ich».
With «wir», the form is «sind». The form «seid» belongs to «ihr».
With «ihr», you all, the form is «seid». It is the only one that ends in «d» other than «sind».

itens.enunciado: To talk to a stranger, politely, use:
itens.explicacao: The formal address is «Sie», with a capital S. The «du» is for people you are close to and the «ihr» is for several people you are close to.

itens.enunciado: To talk to a friend, use:
itens.explicacao: The informal address, for one person you are close to, is «du». «Sie» is formal, and «er» means he, so it is not a way of addressing someone directly.

blocos.enunciado: Say out loud: «Ich bin müde. Du bist hier. Wir sind glücklich.». Then ask two yes/no questions with «sein»: one to a friend, «Bist du müde?», and one to a stranger, «Sind Sie müde?».

Look at the tables of the verbs «heißen» and «kommen» from the previous session and say the personal pronouns out loud with their translation: «ich», «du», «er», «sie», «es», «wir», «ihr», «sie» and «Sie».
